summary.one_line: A profitable, low-leverage alternatives manager (private credit and infrastructure/real-asset funds) with about Rs 48,600 cr of fee-paying AUM. The IPO is a pure Rs 1,200 cr offer for sale by the Edelweiss parent, so the company raises nothing. The business is good, but earnings quality depends on lumpy carry-type income, cash conversion has been weak, and the group's governance record is mixed.
bull_points: Real scale in a niche that is still growing. AUM is about Rs 95,345 cr and fee-paying AUM about Rs 48,623 cr (30 Jun 2026). Fee-paying AUM compounded at about 23.4% a year over FY24-FY26 (S5, S7).

Most revenue is recurring. Management fees were 80.8%-98.1% of annual recurring (ARR) revenue in FY22 to H1 FY25 (S1), and fees are charged on long-dated, closed-end commitments locked for 4.5-10 years (S1).
Profitable every year with modest leverage. FY26 PAT was Rs 265.2 cr on total income of Rs 963.8 cr, ROE was 25.97%, and debt/equity fell from 0.61 (FY24) to 0.41 (FY26) and 0.34 (Jun 2026) (S4, S5).
Growth has picked up recently. Q1 FY27 revenue from operations rose 44.4% YoY to Rs 275.5 cr and PAT rose 45% to Rs 80.7 cr (S2).
A 15+ year track record, with most large funds now in their second or third series, plus an in-house portfolio operating arm (Sekura) running roads, transmission and solar assets (S1).
bear_points: 100% offer for sale. All Rs 1,200 cr goes to promoter Edelweiss Securities & Investments, and the company gets no proceeds (S2, S3).

Profit depends on Variable Additional Return (VAR, a carry-like gain). VAR was 57.5% of total revenue in FY23 and 22.4% in FY24, and PAT fell 45.6% from FY23 to FY24 when it dropped (S1). Of Rs 684.72 cr of VAR recognised since FY24, only Rs 397.65 cr had been realised in cash (S7).
Weak cash conversion. Operating cash flow was -Rs 113.6 cr in FY23, +Rs 10.5 cr in FY24 and -Rs 67.8 cr in H1 FY25, against PAT of Rs 322.2 cr, Rs 175.2 cr and Rs 123.7 cr (S1).

Governance baggage at group and company level. SEBI's case over the company's own stressed-assets AIF (ESTAR) was settled for about Rs 61.4 lakh, with officers-in-default barred for 12 months (S14). In 2024 the RBI acted against group firms over evergreening that used connected AIFs (S16).
PAT margin on total income has slipped each year: 29.98% (FY24), 29.21% (FY25), 27.52% (FY26) and 24.01% (Q1 FY27) (S5, S7).
watch_points: How much of the recognised VAR turns into cash, and whether operating cash flow turns durably positive after listing (S1, S7).
Any further SEBI action. The RHP refers to a pending settlement application with SEBI (S20).
Fundraising pace for successor funds. Annual fund raise swung from Rs 911 cr (FY22) to Rs 13,797 cr (FY23) and Rs 9,687 cr (FY24) (S1).
Promoter group still holds 83.88% after the IPO (S4), which leaves room for future sell-downs. Anchor lock-ins end on 28 Nov 2026 (50%) and 27 Jan 2027 (rest) (S8).

reasoning: The money does nothing for the business. This is a 100% offer for sale by Edelweiss Securities & Investments, a subsidiary of Edelweiss Financial Services (S2, S3). An investor is buying part of the parent's stake, not funding growth. The business is already self-funding and deleveraging (borrowings fell from Rs 507.49 cr in FY25 to Rs 399.20 cr in Jun 2026) (S8), so this alone does not rule it out.

The business is real and of reasonable quality. It has about Rs 48,623 cr of fee-paying AUM growing at roughly 23% a year (S7), ROE in the mid-to-high 20s (S5), management fees making up 80%+ of recurring revenue (S1), and a track record of raising successor fund series (S1). The moat is a modest one: track record and global LP relationships. There is no regulatory or technical barrier, and the DRHP lists ICICI Venture, Kotak Alternate, 360 ONE and others running the same strategies (S1).

Earnings quality is the main analytical problem. Reported profit includes fair-value VAR that is lumpy (FY23 PAT Rs 322 cr, FY24 Rs 175 cr) (S1) and only partly realised (Rs 397.65 cr of Rs 684.72 cr since FY24) (S7). Operating cash flow was negative in two of the last four reported periods in the DRHP (S1). Until RHP-period cash flows show conversion, the growth story rests partly on accounting gains.

The governance record keeps this off an 'invest' call. SEBI alleged that the company had run its ESTAR AIF inconsistently with the placement memorandum and had given the trustee inaccurate information. The case was settled without admission, with a 12-month bar on officers-in-default (S14). The RBI's 2024 action against sister firms ECL Finance and Edelweiss ARC cited evergreening using connected AIFs (S16), though it was lifted in December 2024 (S15). SEBI also returned the first DRHP over reclassification between revenue lines (S13).

Promoter-linked related-party flows are material. The holding company was a fee payer of Rs 43.2 cr in H1 FY25, about 10% of revenue from operations (S1). The group also supplied distribution, loans and asset-management rights (S1). These look disclosed and mostly routine for a group structure, but they need watching once the company is listed.

Net: a decent franchise, but there is no fresh capital, earnings quality is open to question and the group has a regulatory history. Track it for two or three listed quarters, focusing on VAR realisation, operating cash flow, and the closure of the pending SEBI settlement, before committing money.

blocks.text: EAAA is the alternative-investment arm of the Edelweiss group. It was incorporated in 2008 and renamed from Edelweiss Alternative Asset Advisors in August 2024 (S1, S3). It does not lend or invest mainly from its own balance sheet. It raises money from investors (LPs) into closed-end Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), InvITs and co-investment PMS accounts, invests that money, and earns fees plus a performance share. Its two verticals are Private Credit (performing credit, special situations, real estate credit, and core or investment-grade credit) and Real Assets (infrastructure yield, commercial real estate yield, perpetual capital/InvITs, and energy transition) (S1, S2).

As of 30 June 2026 it reported total AUM (capital committed to active funds) of about Rs 95,345 cr, fee-paying AUM of about Rs 48,623 cr, 11,009 client relationships and 277 employees (S4, S5, S7). The gap between total and fee-paying AUM matters. Roughly half of headline AUM does not earn fees, so revenue tracks fee-paying AUM, not the headline number (S4).

blocks.caption: AUM by strategy, Sept 2024 (latest split in the DRHP; Rs cr, converted from Rs mn) (S1)

blocks.text: The mix is shifting towards Real Assets. Their share of ARR AUM rose from 14.8% in FY22 to 40.1% in September 2024 (S1). Private Credit remains the larger pool, with 167 investments and 96 complete exits since inception (S1). The real-asset funds own and run 1.74 mn sq ft of offices, 3,477 lane-km of roads, 1,835 circuit-km of transmission lines and 1.28 GW of solar (S1).

The DRHP splits revenue into two streams (S1). (i) ARR revenue is the management fee net of distribution costs, plus net income on the company's own general-partner or sponsor commitments. (ii) Variable Additional Return (VAR) is the company's share of gains above fund hurdles under each fund's waterfall, booked as fair-value gains. Fees are charged on commitments, drawn capital, invested capital, NAV or gross asset value, depending on the fund (S1). Management fees made up 98.12%, 90.12%, 85.78% and 80.83% of ARR revenue in FY22, FY23, FY24 and H1 FY25 respectively (S1).

blocks.caption: Revenue mix: recurring vs carry-like income (Rs cr, from DRHP KPI table) (S1)

blocks.text: VAR is the swing factor. One qualifying fund drove FY23's Rs 371 cr VAR, and its fall in FY24 cut PAT by 45.6% even though recurring revenue grew 40% (S1). Since FY24 the company has recognised Rs 684.72 cr of VAR but realised only Rs 397.65 cr in cash (S7). Treat VAR-heavy quarters as non-repeatable.

Costs are mostly people. Employee costs were Rs 216.7 cr in FY24, including a Rs 33.1 cr provision for staff's share of VAR. Selling and distribution was Rs 51.3 cr and finance costs Rs 36.5 cr (S1). Senior investment heads share in VAR. The heads of private credit and real assets were paid Rs 8.23 cr and Rs 8.08 cr in FY24 (S1), which aligns them with performance but also means carry leaks to staff.

The clients are the investors in the funds. In September 2024 the top 10 clients contributed 44.78% of AUM (S1), and 52.33% of AUM came from investors outside India: North America 25.2%, Europe 20.7% and rest of world 6.4% (S1). The institutional share of AUM fell from 73.08% in FY22 to 54.83% in September 2024 (S1) and to 49.32% by June 2026 (S5, S7). Over the same period, client relationships grew from 3,682 to 11,009 (S1, S5) as the firm pushed into HNIs and family offices through distributors.

items: Sourcing and investing: an investment team of 79 professionals (September 2024) (S1).
Asset operations: subsidiary Sekura India Management runs portfolio assets (44-person team, ISO 14001/45001/27001/55001 processes) in 16 states (S1, S5).
Fundraising: a 15-person coverage team plus distributors. Offices are in Mumbai, New Delhi, GIFT City and Singapore (S1, S9).
Regulatory capital: as an AIF manager it must keep a sponsor stake (for Category I/II AIFs, 2.5% of corpus or Rs 5 cr), which ties up balance sheet (S1).

blocks.caption: Track record of the three largest funds per vertical, Sept 2024 (S1)

blocks.text: The DRHP's commissioned CARE report puts India's alternatives AUM at about US$130.7 bn in 2022, up from US$58.4 bn in 2014. It expects private credit plus real assets, EAAA's two segments, to reach about US$107.5 bn by 2028, rising from 38% of the alternatives industry in 2023 to 45% (S1). RHP-period summaries cite AIF commitments of Rs 16.9 trillion in FY26, about 129 times the FY14 level, with SEBI-registered AIFs, REITs and InvITs compounding at 29.5% over FY19-FY26 (S5).

On the Q1 FY27 call, Edelweiss management put alternatives AUM at about 3.5% of India's GDP versus about 27% in the US. It cited a projected rise in industry AUM from US$166 bn to about US$276 bn, with income/yield strategies growing about 18% a year (S17). These are industry-level, commissioned or management figures and should be read as the bull case for the sector, not as a forecast for EAAA.

blocks.caption: India alternatives AUM by segment, US$ bn (CARE report via DRHP) (S1)

blocks.text: Private credit is the fastest-growing segment in that data, rising from US$3.7 bn to US$19.5 bn between 2014 and 2022 (S1). Real assets grew far more slowly, from US$21.5 bn to US$27.4 bn (S1). The DRHP also cites about Rs 110 trillion of domestic institutional capital with little allocation to alternatives so far (S1). That is the structural opportunity, but the timing depends on regulation.

The DRHP's own peer map lists ICICI Venture, Kotak Alternate Asset Managers and 360 ONE as running both real-asset and private-credit strategies. SBICAP Ventures, True North and Vivriti compete in private credit, and Motilal Oswal and Axis AMC in parts of the market (S1). The DRHP also notes competition from global institutional funds investing in India with more capital (S1). The offer document's listed peer set (360 ONE WAM, HDFC AMC, Nippon Life AMC, ABSL AMC, UTI AMC, ICICI Prudential AMC, Anand Rathi Wealth, Nuvama, Gaja Alternative Asset) is mostly mutual fund or wealth businesses, which reviewers say is not a like-for-like comparison (S7, S11). Gaja is the only other listed pure alternatives manager (S6).

Listed comparables for a pure-play Indian private-credit and infrastructure manager effectively don't exist. That cuts both ways: scarcity value for institutions, and little external benchmark for a retail investor.

In fundraising, the competition is concentrated at the top. Per CARE, large alternatives managers raised about US$28 bn over the past decade, and the top three took about 70% of it (S1). EAAA places itself among the leaders, which is plausible given fund series of more than Rs 10,000 cr, such as EISAF II and ISAF III (S1). For global LP money, though, it competes with global managers and their India platforms, which the DRHP acknowledges have more deployable capital (S1).

There is some moat, but it is modest. The real advantages are: (i) a long, auditable track record across fund series, which institutional LPs require before committing (most large funds are in their second or third series) (S1); (ii) multi-year closed-end commitments that lock fees in for 4.5-10 years (S1); (iii) an operating platform (Sekura) that lets it buy and run operating infrastructure, which pure lenders cannot do (S1); and (iv) global LP relationships, with about US$3.76 bn committed by global institutions as of September 2024 (S1). The DRHP says onboarding global institutions is a 'prolonged process' that is hard to replicate (S1). That is fair, but it is a barrier of time and reputation, not a regulatory or technical one.

items: No licence scarcity: SEBI AIF and PMS registrations are widely held, and the DRHP lists at least eight domestic rivals (S1).
The claim to be 'one of the leading alternatives platforms in India by AUM' rests on a report the company commissioned and paid for (CARE) (S1).

The reputation moat is exposed to group events. The 2024 RBI evergreening action named connected AIFs (S16), and SEBI's ESTAR settlement concerned an EAAA-managed fund (S14). Damage there would hit the very asset (LP trust) the moat depends on.

blocks.text: Verdict on moat: modest and real, based on track record, successor-fund economics and LP relationships. It is not a structural moat, and it depends on reputation, which is where this group has been weakest.

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated financials, Rs cr (S4, S5, S6, S7, S8)

blocks.text: Total income grew 34.6% in FY25 and 22.5% in FY26, and PAT grew 31.2% and 15.4% (S4, S6). Fee-paying AUM grew only 11.3% in FY25, then 32.1% in FY26 (S24), so FY25's profit growth ran ahead of its fee base, probably helped by VAR. Q1 FY27 shows revenue from operations up 44.4% and PAT up 45% YoY (S2). Management said the EYIP One fund exit contributed carry income in that quarter (S17).

Margins are moving the wrong way. PAT margin fell from 29.98% to 27.52% over FY24-FY26 and to 24.01% in Q1 FY27 (S5, S7). On revenue from operations, net margin fell from 35.56% to 30.50% (S6, S21). Growth in income is not yet producing operating leverage.

subsections.title: The longer view: what the 2024 DRHP shows

blocks.text: The December 2024 DRHP, which SEBI returned (S13), adds FY22-FY23 and shows how volatile earnings can be. Total income went from Rs 216.0 cr (FY22) to Rs 701.2 cr (FY23) and back down to Rs 584.3 cr (FY24). PAT went Rs 48.9 cr, Rs 322.2 cr, then Rs 175.2 cr (S1). The FY23 spike came from Rs 371 cr of VAR on one qualifying fund (S1). FY24 revenue from operations in that document was Rs 583.85 cr, against Rs 492.58 cr in RHP-era coverage, while total income is the same Rs 584.25 cr (S1, S6). That gap fits a reclassification between revenue lines, which is the issue SEBI cited when it returned the first draft (S13).

blocks.caption: Profit vs operating cash flow, from the 2024 DRHP (Rs cr) (S1)

blocks.text: Cash-flow/profit mismatch. Over FY22 to H1 FY25, cumulative PAT was about Rs 670 cr while cumulative operating cash flow was about -Rs 135 cr (computed from S1). Part of this is structural, because VAR is a non-cash fair-value gain and sponsor commitments absorb cash (S1). It still means reported profit has not yet turned into distributable cash at the same rate. RHP-period (FY25-FY26) cash flows could not be verified for this report.

Leverage is low and falling. The borrowings fund sponsor commitments and co-investments, not lending (S1). Trade receivables were Rs 166.90 cr (Mar 2026) and Rs 154.46 cr (Jun 2026), and contingent liabilities were Rs 37.70 cr (S7). The company paid a 640% dividend for FY26 and 190% so far in FY27 (S7). On a Rs 5 face value and 6.47 cr shares (S5), that is roughly Rs 207 cr for FY26 (computed), about 78% of FY26 PAT, and about 95% of it went to the promoter group, which held 95.03% before the IPO (S4). That is heavy upstreaming to the parent ahead of listing, at a time when operating cash flow has been thin.

blocks.text: SEBI returned the first DRHP (December 2024) on 27 March 2025 over observations on reclassification between revenue lines (S13). The company refiled on 19 January 2026, received SEBI's observations on 23 April 2026, and filed the RHP dated 19 October 2026 (S12, S20). In March 2026, Edelweiss also placed 4.4% of EAAA with existing LPs and select individuals for about Rs 375 cr (S19).

The issue size was cut by 20%, from Rs 1,500 cr in the DRHP to Rs 1,200 cr in the RHP (S4, S10). The 2024 DRHP had also provided for an employee reservation (up to 5% of post-offer capital) and an EFSL-shareholder reservation (up to 10% of offer size) (S1). Category tables published for the live issue show only QIB, NII and retail buckets (S8), so check the RHP's offer structure before applying through either quota.
Eligibility route: the 2024 DRHP filed under SEBI ICDR Regulation 6(1), the profitability-track-record route, which is why retail gets 35% and QIBs 50% (S1, S7).

subsections.title: Objects of the offer: where the money goes

blocks.caption: Use of proceeds (S1, S2, S11)
rows: Edelweiss Securities & Investments (promoter selling shareholder), net of its share of offer expenses and taxes
Fresh issue (capex, debt repayment, working capital, GCP)
Carry out the OFS; achieve benefits of listing

blocks.text: EAAA receives nothing. The listing monetises the parent's stake. Edelweiss Financial Services is the selling group, and its stated aim is to list its businesses separately over time (S17). The share count is unchanged at 6,46,55,246 before and after the issue (S5), so no dilution occurs, but no new capital comes in either.

For context on the seller's gain, the December 2024 DRHP certified the selling shareholder's weighted average cost of acquisition at Rs 54.45 per share (S1). This is a reminder that the offer is an exit, not a capital raise. It is not a valuation argument either way.

The promoters are Edelweiss Financial Services (EFSL), Edelweiss Securities & Investments (ESIPL, the holding company and seller), Edel Finance Company and Edelweiss Global Wealth Management (S1, S4). Rashesh Shah, an EFSL co-founder associated with EFSL since 1995, is non-executive Chairman. Venkatchalam Ramaswamy, also an EFSL co-founder, has run business operations and fundraising since 2010 and became MD & CEO in 2024 on Rs 3 cr fixed pay, a bonus of up to Rs 6 cr and up to Rs 3 cr of perquisites, with possible VAR participation (S1). The 2024 board had eight directors, four of them independent (S1).

blocks.caption: Key managers (from the DRHP) (S1)
rows: President, head of private credit (ex-PwC, ARCIL)
President, head of real assets (ex-IDBI, Axis)

blocks.text: The investment heads have long tenures (2011-2017) and relevant credit or infrastructure backgrounds (S1), which is a strength. Regretted attrition fell from 21.86% in FY23 to 8.88% in FY24 (S1). Fund documents carry key-person clauses that can suspend capital calls if named people leave (S1), so retaining Ramaswamy, Agarwal and Chordia is a real business dependency.

The DRHP's RPT schedule is long because EAAA sits inside a group of NBFCs, an ARC, insurers and a former broking affiliate. Most items are routine shared services, such as cost reimbursements to Edelweiss Rural & Corporate Services (Rs 10.95 cr in FY24) and group insurance (S1). Several items are material enough to watch, though.

items: Fee income from the holding company ESIPL was Rs 17.1 cr in FY24 and Rs 43.2 cr in H1 FY25, about 10% of H1 FY25 revenue from operations (computed from S1). Fees were also earned from group entities ECL Finance (Rs 4.2 cr) and India Credit Investment Fund III (Rs 12.3 cr) in FY24 (S1).

Group distribution: fund-raising distributor expenses ran through Nuvama Wealth, a former group associate (Rs 19.5 cr expensed in FY23, plus Rs 171.0 cr recorded as prepaid), and Edelweiss Global Wealth Management (S1).
Group funding: term loans of Rs 22 cr each from EFSL and ERCSL in FY24 (repaid), and Rs 230 cr of CCDs issued to ESIPL in FY23 (S1).

Asset transfers: EAAA bought asset-management rights (Rs 21.3 cr) and AIF sponsor units (Rs 3.3 cr) from Edelweiss Asset Management, and VAR rights (Rs 4.9 cr) from ESIPL, in H1 FY25. It also bought unquoted equity from EFSL (Rs 213.4 cr) and ESIPL (Rs 11.1 cr) in FY23 (S1).
Advisory fee paid to group NBFC ECL Finance: Rs 5.7 cr in FY24 (S1).

blocks.text: Read these with the group context. The RBI's May 2024 action found group entities 'acting in concert' through structured transactions using Edelweiss ARC and connected AIFs to evergreen ECL Finance's stressed loans (S16). The RPTs above are disclosed and may well be arm's length, but they come from the same group web. The 2026 RHP's updated RPT schedule could not be opened for this report.

items: ESTAR AIF case (company-level): SEBI issued a show-cause notice on 12 July 2024 to EAAA and its Edelweiss Stressed and Troubled Assets Revival Fund. It alleged that the fund did not act in investors' interest, that EAAA ran the fund inconsistently with its placement memorandum, and that EAAA gave the trustee inaccurate information (FY2016-17 compliance report). The case was settled without admission for about Rs 61.4 lakh, with officers-in-default barred from the company for 12 months. EAAA added an independent fund board and a conflicts committee (S1, S14).
The RHP states that a settlement application with SEBI on an ongoing matter is still pending (S20). The details could not be verified for this report.

Earlier SEBI inspections had flagged deficiencies at EAAA funds: compliance standards, delayed quarterly reports to contributors, and missing corporate approvals for lower-IRR divestments (S1). The RBI compounded a 9-day FC-GPR filing delay for a Rs 14,167 penalty (April 2024) (S1).

Group: the RBI's May 2024 restrictions on ECL Finance and Edelweiss ARC (S16) were lifted on 17 December 2024 after remediation (S15). Promoter EFSL settled a SEBI summary proceeding on NCD incentives for Rs 19.50 lakh (S1).

Directors: pending criminal complaints and FIRs name Rashesh Shah, including a 2008 FIR (with Ramaswamy) over Rs 0.85 cr of F&O trades and an August 2024 FIR alleging criminal breach of trust. There is also a 2021 Enforcement Directorate show-cause notice involving Ramaswamy as a former ERCSL executive (FEMA, pulse imports) (S1). All are pending or responded to, and none is adjudicated.

blocks.text: The pattern is the concern rather than any single item. The company has a settled SEBI case over its own AIF's governance, a group-level evergreening action, a returned DRHP and multiple pending matters against the chairman. None is disqualifying alone, but together they justify a governance discount and close monitoring.

items: 1. Earnings quality and VAR lumpiness. VAR made up 57.5% of total revenue in FY23 and 22.4% in FY24 (S1). PAT fell 45.6% in FY24 when VAR fell (S1), and only Rs 397.65 cr of Rs 684.72 cr VAR recognised since FY24 has been realised (S7). VAR can also be clawed back, up to 100% of amounts distributed, in specified cases (S1).
2. Weak cash conversion. Cumulative operating cash flow was negative over FY22 to H1 FY25 while cumulative PAT was about Rs 670 cr (S1).

3. Fundraising cyclicality. Fund raises are lumpy: Rs 911 cr (FY22), Rs 13,797 cr (FY23), Rs 9,687 cr (FY24) and Rs 1,684 cr (H1 FY25) (S1). Future fees depend on closing successor funds, and the DRHP flags that interest in alternatives can fade with rates and sentiment (S1, S11).

4. Client concentration and offshore dependence. The top 10 clients held 44.78% of AUM and foreign clients 52.33% (Sept 2024) (S1). Losing one large global LP, or a turn against India, would hit successor fundraising.

5. Credit and valuation risk in the funds. Fund assets are illiquid, Level-3 valued and partly in distressed sectors. The DRHP warns that realised values can fall materially below NAV marks, which would reverse VAR (S1).

blocks.text: Risks 1 and 2 are really one issue seen from two sides. A large part of reported profit is a mark-to-model share of fund gains that arrives in cash only on exits, if at all (S1, S7). For a retail shareholder, management-fee earnings on fee-paying AUM are the dependable core, and VAR is an option whose value is real but uncertain.

The 2024 DRHP lists the company's own litigation as small: 2 tax matters and 1 regulatory action, totalling Rs 1.8 cr. Promoters face 39 tax proceedings totalling about Rs 231 cr (S1). Neither is a balance-sheet threat to EAAA. The bigger risk is reputational, not financial.

items: 6. Group and regulatory contagion. The ESTAR settlement (S14), the RBI evergreening action citing connected AIFs (S16) and a still-pending SEBI settlement application (S20) mean further regulatory findings could damage LP trust, which is the core asset.
7. Key-person risk. Fund agreements can suspend capital calls or end investment periods if named key persons leave (S1), and senior staff pay is tied to VAR (S1).

8. Promoter overhang and no fresh capital. The issue is 100% OFS (S2), and the promoter group retains 83.88% (S4). Further secondary sales by a parent that has been upstreaming cash (FY26 dividend of 640%) (S7) are likely over time.

blocks.text: Generic DRHP risks such as macro conditions, tax law changes, technology and cybersecurity have been left out. These eight are the ones that could plausibly change the investment decision.

One mitigating point: the DRHP says clients have not failed to honour capital calls so far, and that no losses at overall fund level occurred in the 3.5 years before filing (S1). That is a short window, but there is no history of fund-level blow-ups at the platform.

items: ROE: management targets a 'sustainable' 25-35% ROE, against about 26% in FY26 and 29% in Q1 FY27 (S17).

Carry pipeline: funds raised about eight years ago are entering exit mode. EYIP One was exited in Q1 FY27 and contributed carry, and management said the best returns come after 11-12 years (S17). This points to more VAR in the near term, which is lumpy by nature.
Yields: PAT yield on fee-paying AUM was 0.69% and total-income yield 2.89% in Q1 FY27. Management argued alternatives earn 50-100 bps PAT yields versus 20-45 bps for mutual funds (S17).
Client mix: roughly 50:50 institutional vs non-institutional, with an expectation that domestic institutional allocation to alternatives will rise, with no timeframe given (S17).

Strategy (DRHP): widen the client base through the in-house coverage team and global distribution, add more income and yield products (energy transition was added in FY25), use technology, and keep active asset management through Sekura (S1).

blocks.text: No numerical revenue, AUM or fundraising guidance was found in the sources reviewed. The Q1 FY27 commentary comes from a third-party AI summary of the Edelweiss call, not a transcript (S17), so treat the exact figures with some caution.

Parent intent matters here. Edelweiss management says it aims to list each of its businesses independently over time (S17), and it sold 4.4% of EAAA before the IPO (S19). Expect the parent to remain a seller of EAAA stock over time.

The forward case is plausible. Fee-paying AUM has grown about 23% a year (S7), recent funds such as IYP II and ISAF III are still early in their lives (S1), and older vintages are maturing into carry (S17). The weak points are that margins are compressing (S5), the extra profit in FY27 is likely to be carry-heavy and therefore uneven, and growth increasingly relies on HNI and distributor channels, which carry higher distribution cost (S1). Watch whether management fees on fee-paying AUM, rather than VAR, carry the growth.
Anything a sell-side IPO note says about 'the alternatives boom' is industry tailwind, not company guidance. EAAA's own commitments are limited to the ROE range and the qualitative strategy above.

items: Metric 1: growth in fee-paying AUM, which was +27% YoY in Q1 FY27 (S17), and whether management-fee revenue keeps pace with it.
Metric 2: VAR realised vs recognised (Rs 397.65 cr of Rs 684.72 cr so far) (S7).
Metric 3: new fund closes in Private Credit. That vertical raised only Rs 66 cr in H1 FY25 against Rs 1,525 cr in Real Assets (S1).

subsections.title: Anchors, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: Anchor book (23 Oct 2026): about Rs 360 cr raised by allotting 21,62,161 shares at Rs 1,665, the top of the band (S9). Ten domestic mutual funds took 61% of the anchor book, including HDFC, ICICI Prudential, SBI, Nippon India and Kotak. Other named anchors include Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, Schroders, Carnelian, 360 ONE, Unifi and Nuvama (S9). Anchor lock-in: 50% until 28 Nov 2026 and the remainder until 27 Jan 2027 (S8).

Day-1 subscription figures (retail/NII/QIB) were not yet published when this was written on the opening day, 26 Oct 2026. Trackers showed blank or placeholder entries (S8). No subscription multiple is implied here.
Grey market premium, unofficial: Investorgain showed Rs 36 at 07:02 AM on 26 Oct 2026, about 2% over the upper band (S18). GMP is unregulated and volatile, and it plays no part in the verdict.

method: Primary source: I read the December 5, 2024 DRHP (S1) page by page. It was downloaded from the lead manager Axis Capital's site, and I covered the offer summary, related-party schedule, risk factors 1-24, Our Business, management/KMP, MD&A including cash flows, and outstanding litigation. SEBI returned that DRHP in March 2025. The refiled January 2026 DRHP (too large to fetch, over 10 MB) and the October 19, 2026 RHP (HTTP 403 on the company, BSE and NSE mirrors) could NOT be opened. So the FY24-FY26 and Q1 FY27 restated figures (revenue, PAT, net worth, borrowings, KPIs, fee-paying AUM, VAR realisation, dividends) come from secondary IPO-analysis pages that quote the RHP. I cross-checked them across at least two of S4, S5, S6, S7 and S8, and the core P&L and balance sheet lines agree across those sources. Not verified: the RHP-period cash flow statement, the updated RPT schedule, the RHP-era litigation and the pending SEBI settlement detail (S20 is a search snippet), and the per-category split of the 72.07 lakh offered shares (S8 shows a 74.6 lakh base). The FY22-H1 FY25 cash flow, VAR mix, client concentration and RPT analysis come from the 2024 DRHP and may be superseded by the RHP. Management outlook comes from a third-party AI summary of the parent's Q1 FY27 call (S17), not a transcript. Day-1 subscription data did not exist at writing. Market cap and all valuation multiples quoted by sources were deliberately excluded. Some figures are computed from the sources (Rs mn converted to Rs cr, cumulative OCF vs PAT, dividend outgo, RPT share of revenue); these are flagged as computed. For undated web pages the date shown is the access date (2026-10-26). Sources marked 'seen in search results' were not opened with WebFetch (paywall or 403) and are cited only for facts shown in search snippets.
